sections.body: Restaurant workers handle ingredients, tools, dishes, and surfaces used by customers. Symptoms such as fever, diarrhea, or vomiting, as well as hand injuries, can increase contamination risks. Each workplace has reporting and task-assignment rules; tell the supervisor so safe duties can be assigned before work begins.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Before your shift, change into your uniform, cover your hair, store personal belongings, and check your hands and general condition. If you feel ill while working, stop handling food and tell the supervisor. Do not hide symptoms or simply put on gloves to continue a risky task.

Practice scenario: Before preparing a salad, a worker feels nauseated and has been vomiting since morning, but the restaurant is busy.
Recommended response: Tell the supervisor, do not prepare food, and wait for a task assignment according to restaurant procedures.

sections.body: Hands, knives, cutting boards, and counters can transfer contamination from raw ingredients to food that will not be cooked again. Wash your hands after touching raw meat, waste, toilets, money, phones, or cleaning tasks. The same gloves can also spread contamination; follow the restaurant's rules for changing gloves and separating equipment.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Store ingredients and cutting boards according to the restaurant's labels or color coding. After preparing raw meat, stop, wash your hands, change gloves if worn, and use a cleaned surface for ready-to-eat food. If a clean tool is exposed to raw juices, set it aside and request rewashing.

Practice scenario: After cutting raw chicken, a worker uses the same gloves to pick up tomato slices for a salad.
Recommended response: Stop serving the salad, separate tools and ingredients that may be affected, wash your hands, and tell the supervisor so they can be handled again.

sections.body: Cold, hot, and ready-to-eat foods have storage requirements based on the product and restaurant plan. Use a thermometer and the limits written for that ingredient rather than relying on touch or memorized numbers. Container lids, time labels, and ingredient separation help maintain safety and quality during a shift.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Check the temperature with the designated instrument, clean the probe according to procedure, and record the time and result. Keep containers covered with readable identification. If the temperature or time exceeds restaurant limits, a label is missing, or equipment does not work, hold the ingredient and ask the supervisor to decide what to do next.

Practice scenario: Soup ready to be served has no time label, and the station thermometer is displaying an error.
Recommended response: Do not serve the soup. Hold the container, report the missing label and faulty instrument, and wait for an inspection according to procedure.

sections.body: Organized preparation reduces ingredient mix-ups, waiting, and repeated movements during busy service. Check the recipe, portions, tools, and ingredient condition before setting up a station. Keep ready-to-eat food separate from raw ingredients; use knives, heat, and electrical equipment only within your training.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Arrange ingredients in labeled containers, take only what is needed for the shift, and store the rest as required. Read tickets carefully; if a note is unreadable, confirm it before cooking. Clean spills promptly without contaminating ingredients or making the floor slippery.

Practice scenario: The ticket is for vegetable soup, but an unlabelled container at the station has unidentified contents.
Recommended response: Do not use the contents. Set the container aside and ask the supervisor to identify them before preparing the order.

sections.body: Food allergies can cause serious reactions. Ingredient information and cross-contact risks can vary by menu, supplier, and cooking method. Use the restaurant's current allergy guide and ask an authorized person when an answer is unclear. Do not guess from a dish's name or claim it is allergen-free without confirmation.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Listen to the ingredient the customer needs to avoid, repeat it to confirm, then check the guide or menu system. Clearly share what is known. If the information is insufficient, tell the customer you will confirm it and contact the supervisor or kitchen right away. Do not change the recipe or ask the kitchen to ignore procedures.

Practice scenario: A customer asks whether a sauce contains peanuts, but the ingredient list at the station has not been updated.
Recommended response: Do not guess. Say you will check, hold off on recommending the dish, and ask the supervisor to verify the latest information.

sections.body: Notes such as “no egg” or “sauce on the side” change how the kitchen prepares and serves a dish. The ticket must state the change clearly and be linked to the correct table or order number. For allergy-related requests, the kitchen follows established cross-contact procedures; do not treat small changes as unimportant.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

Repeat the change to the customer, enter it in the system or ticket, and make sure the kitchen receives the correct version. If tickets are mixed up or a modification is unconfirmed, hold the dish before it is carried out. Use the plate and tools designated for the order; do not simply scrape an ingredient off a finished dish.

Practice scenario: A customer requests an egg-free dish because of an allergy, but the original ticket has already gone to the kitchen without that note.
Recommended response: Do not bring out the original dish. Stop service, tell the kitchen and supervisor, then create the correct ticket and follow allergy procedures.

Greet guests politely, ask the party size when needed, and confirm reservations without saying personal information aloud. Keep service routes clear of carts, belongings, and spills so guests and staff can pass safely.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

Greet guests, listen to their answers, and repeat important information such as the reservation name or party size. If a table is not ready, give an estimated wait only after checking and ask guests to wait in the designated area. Do not promise a particular table without confirming it in the system.

Practice scenario: Guests arrive without a reservation, and a recently vacated table has not yet been cleaned.
Recommended response: Greet them, explain that the table is being prepared, and ask them to wait in the designated area until the table is confirmed ready.

sections.body: Each dish must reach the table and customer who ordered it. Before leaving, read the dish name or number on the ticket, check the quantity and modifications, and make sure the plates and tray are stable. Routes between tables can be narrow; prioritize visibility and balance over speed.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Lift the tray steadily and use a route that is not slippery. At the table, briefly name each dish and set it down without touching the eating surface. If an item does not match the ticket or the customer says it is not what they ordered, do not leave it; hold it and take it back to the check point.

Practice scenario: In the aisle, a worker sees a ticket on the tray for table 8, but a colleague calls them to table 6.
Recommended response: Stop in a safe place and match the ticket to the table number; do not hand over the dish until its destination is confirmed.

sections.body: Complaints may concern an incorrect dish, delays, quality, allergies, or safety. Stay calm, listen without arguing, apologize for the inconvenience, and gather the facts. Replacements, refunds, and incident handling must follow the restaurant's authority rules; immediately refer health concerns to the supervisor.

sections.body:

sections.body: Accurate payment depends on the table bill, amount, payment method, and cashier procedures. Check the total in the system and explain charges clearly if customers ask. Handle cash, cards, and payment apps as instructed; do not store passwords, card numbers, or customer information outside the official system.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Before closing a transaction, match the table number and items on the bill. State the amount due, process the customer's chosen payment method, and provide a receipt if the system requires it. If a payment is declined or the amount differs, do not retry until the first transaction's status is confirmed; call the supervisor or follow cashier procedures.

Practice scenario: The payment terminal shows a pending message after the customer taps their card, and the customer asks the worker to try again.
Recommended response: Check the transaction status in the system or ask the supervisor before retrying, so the customer is not charged twice.

sections.body: Closing a restaurant includes cleaning tools and tables, storing ingredients, disposing of waste, and checking remaining tasks. Store ingredients according to their labels and required conditions; keep cleaning chemicals separate. Shift handover notes should identify low stock, damaged equipment, held ingredients, and unfinished tasks.
sections.title: Work Concepts and Standards

sections.body:
Follow the closing checklist from clean areas to dirty areas using the appropriate cleaning tools. Make sure ingredients are packed, labeled, and placed in the correct storage location. Before leaving, tell the next shift about low stock or equipment problems; do not mark work complete if it has not been done.

Practice scenario: At the end of a shift, an open ingredient container has no time label and refrigerator cleaning has not been recorded.
Recommended response: Set the container aside for assessment according to rules, record the unfinished cleaning, and hand both items over to the supervisor.
